content.confidence: 2: You are willing to defend your assessment, but it is quite likely that you did not understand the central parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: In the SAT problem, we are given a conjunctive normal form (CNF) formula and the goal is to determine whether this formula is satisfiable (i.e. the formula is true for at least one variable assignment), or not. This paper focuses on CNF instances that are known to be unsatisfiable, and the goal is to find a small backtrack search tree. To this end, a Monte-Carlo Forest Search (MCFS) algorithm is proposed, by coupling the Monte Carlo Tree Search algorithm, Knuth’s algorithm for estimating tree sizes, and a pre-existing solver for handling small subtrees. The performance of this framework is evaluated on two distributions of SAT instances.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Arguably, the main strength of this paper is of empirical nature. The MCFS algorithm is competitive with the best solvers on the *random* and the *sgen* distributions.

Unfortunately, the paper has, in its current state, several weaknesses: 

**Novelty:** the paper is essentially combining existing methods for solving SAT instances. Notably, the MCTS approach was already advocated for SAT solving (see e.g. Keszocze et. al. 2020). Furthermore, the Knuth sampling method for tree size estimation has already been well-studied in the literature, wherein various refinements of this method have been proposed (see e.g. Purdom, 1978; Chen, 1992; Lobjois and Lemaitre 1998; Cornuéjols et. al. 2006, etc.).

**Clarity:** the overall MCFS framework is only explained at a coarse-grained level. Notably, various neural networks are used to estimate the branching policy (Page 5), the value of leaves (Page 5), and the solver performance (Page 6). Virtually nothing is said about the architecture and the hyper-parameters of these neural models. 

**Soundness:** estimating the tree size of a branching policy using Knuth’s sampling can yield technical issues (see comment below).

**References:**

Chen, P. 1992. Heuristic sampling: a method for predicting the performance of tree searching programs. SIAM Journal of Computing 21(2):295–315.

Cornuéjols, G., Karamanov, M., & Li, Y. (2006). Early Estimates of the Size of Branch-and-Bound Trees. INFORMS J. Comput., 18, 86-96.

Lobjois, L., and Lemaitre, M. 1998. Branch and bound algorithm selection by performance prediction. In Proc. of 15th National Conf. on Artificial Intelligence, 353–358. AAAI.

Purdom, P. 1978. Tree size by partial backtracking. SIAM Journal of Computing 7(4):481–491.

Keszocze, O., Schmitz, K., Schloeter, J., Drechsler, R. (2020). Improving SAT Solving Using Monte Carlo Tree Search-Based Clause Learning. In: Drechsler, R., Soeken, M. (eds) Advanced Boolean Techniques. Springer
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
See the above comments about clarity and novelty issues.

The problem considered in Section 4.1 is the following. Given a CNF instance $S$ and a branching policy $\phi$, what is the size of the resulting search tree $T_{\phi}(S)$?  In order to address this problem, the authors are using Knuth’s technique: starting at the root of a search tree $T$, Knuth’s algorithm extends a partial path by expanding the end node and picking a child according to a uniform distribution (over children). It then forms an unbiased estimate of the tree property using the branching degrees along the randomly selected path. 

The key issue with this sampling technique lies in its high variance, especially for heavy-tailed distributions which frequently occur in SAT problems. In order to handle this issue, the authors are using multiple random paths, instead of just one. But how many paths are required in order to significantly reduce the variance? Since this is one of the core ideas of this paper, a bound on variance reduction should be provided here. Furthermore, a comparison of this “multi-sampling” approach with other well-studied variants of Knuth’s algorithm (e.g. Purdom, 1978; Chen, 1992) should also be provided.
content.summary_of_the_review: To sum up, the Monte Carlo Forest Search approach looks empirically promising for handling random UNSAT instances, but the overall architecture is essentially juxtaposing existing techniques. Furthermore, the clarity of the paper should be improved and some statistical guarantees for the multi-sampling extension of Knuth's probing should be provided, together with a detailed comparison with alternative sampling techniques.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.title: Response to Reviewer AVmx
content.comment:
[Novelty] The author’s main concern is about novelty: “the paper is essentially combining existing methods for solving SAT instances”.  The reviewer provided many relevant references that we missed. This was a major blind spot of our related work that we have now filled in. We certainly should have engaged with these papers, however we don’t think these papers impact our novelty claims. We address the references for “MCTS for SAT solving” and “Knuth alternatives” below. We have added text to the related work and made some modifications to clarify our contributions in the introduction and methods sections.

[MCTS advocated for SAT solving (see e.g. Keszocze et. al. 2020) ]: Yes, there are several examples of MCTS being used as an algorithm for directly searching for a satisfying solution to a CSP. There are two main differences we see with these approaches relative to ours: (1) MCTS is being used online for solving CSP rather than as an offline procedure for training a model-based branching policy and (2) these approaches are not designed for the unsatisfiable case where policies produce trees rather than paths. Does this clarification help distinguish our method from this branch of literature? We added the following text to the related work to describe these approaches:

In these uses of online MCTS for solving CSP, a lookahead can be interpreted as a guess at a satisfying assignment. If an unseen node is reached or a conflict is reached along a lookahead path, a reward is assigned based on a proxy measure of how close the path is to being a satisfying assignment (e.g., number of satisfied constraints). These MCTS approaches lie somewhere between local search and DPLL. 

Previti et al. (2011) developed UCTSAT, which assigns 0 reward to a conflict node and explores various alternatives for value estimation such as (1) number of satisfied clauses at current state and (2) average number of satisfied clauses based on random paths from that state. A number of follow-up works have incorporated clause learning into UCTSAT. Schloeter (2017) adds new clauses to the problem for every conflict that is encountered. This addition does not affect the UCT tree since state is defined as the set of assigned variables and therefore independent of additional clauses. Keszocze et al. (2020) make better use of the learned clauses by filtering out any expanded nodes that are ruled out by a learned clause. They modify Previti et al.’s reward function by weighting each satisfied clause by its activity (number of times occurring in resolution) and propose a number of other variations including penalizing by the depth of conflict. We penalize by $2^{depth}$, which corresponds to minimizing the size of the proof tree. Loth et al. (2013) developed a version of UCTSAT for Constraint Programming (CP) that was simplified to be state independent. Rather than each tree node representing a different multi-armed bandit (MAB), they have a single MAB that they update at every node of the tree. This change was made to incorporate restarts, where there would be too few samples for each node. They reward a path by the length until conflict. Wattez et al. (2020) use a single MAB to choose which branching heuristic to use on a given instance. They reward a path to a conflict by the number of assignments ruled out by that path.


[Various refinements to Knuth have been proposed / should compare against]: We found that Knuth samples allowed us to “turn trees into paths” and directly get Monte Carlo estimations of tree size. We don’t claim that this is the best way but we show empirical evidence that this approximation allowed us to learn an improved branching policy. We saw no obvious way of incorporating other “multisampling” approximations into MCTS. We added the following text to our paper:

A Knuth sample provides a path-based rollout, which allows us to easily leverage MCTS. There has been extensive follow-up work developing alternatives for approximating tree size (e.g., Purdom, 1978; Chen, 1992; Cornuejols et al., 2006; Kilby et al., 2006), but these estimates are not decomposed into path-based rollouts from root to leaf, and require new ideas to be integrated into MCFS.

[Missing architecture / hyper-params]: We don’t describe in the main body but we do have a detailed description in the appendix (we mention this at the beginning Section 5). See Appendix B for a detailed description of our architecture / hyper params and training procedure. We will move into the main text for the final submission.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces MCFS (Monte Carlo Forest Search), a new algorithm developed to identify small search trees among a forest of tree candidates, which are recursively built to show that a constraint satisfaction problem has no solution. Among all the possible trees, it is interesting to directly build the smallest one without having to consider them all. The main contribution of this paper is to use a Monte Carlo method to approximate the size of trees without deploying the whole trees recursively. It was proposed by Knuth in 1975 and consists in sampling a path from the root to the leaves and using its length to estimate the size of the tree. The method also uses a solver at a depth set by the user. The overall approach is evaluated on the Boolean satisfiability problem.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
I am not familiar with the family of issues (proof trees of unsatisfiability) addressed by this article and discovered them while reading it. I found the problem interesting and the developed approach clearly deserves some attention. However, it also suffers from a number of drawbacks.

It is possible that I have misunderstood but the problem seems to me badly posed. It appears to me that one searches for a small proof tree to minimize the computation time. However, finding the smallest tree (which will certainly be explored quickly) but in a very long time may not be interesting compared to a naive approach which will explore a bigger tree but without the cost of choosing the tree. In the paper, two ideas are facing each other: tree size estimation and speeding up the computation time. However, it is clear that an accurate estimation takes more time and a compromise has to be investigated. I would like the authors to clearly and formally state the problem they are trying to solve. If the goal is to find the smallest tree as the title suggests, I would have appreciated to read theoretical or empirical results on this specific point.

The authors rightly note that the Monte Carlo estimate of the tree size has probably a large variance and repeatedly mention the importance of seeking to reduce it. This interesting issue is only superficially addressed in the paper since there is no study, neither theoretical nor empirical, of the variance and of the means used to reduce it. This problem is also related to the previous point (as noticed by the authors in the second footnote, but again without detailed explanations).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: From my point of view, the paper is difficult to read for non-specialists of constraint satisfaction problems. Moreover, the presentation follows the very empirical construction of the algorithm without the required formal presentation of the problem at hand, especially in subsections 4.2, 4.3 and 4.4. Some details (such as the construction of the neural networks and how they are trained) are missing.
content.summary_of_the_review: I think the problem and the approach of this paper are interesting and in the scope of the conference. But a thorough rewriting seems to me necessary. In particular, an introduction for non-specialists of this type of problem and a formalization of the problem addressed would be very appreciated. The authors may object that there is section 3, but on the one hand it comes late and on the other hand it does not completely fulfill its objectives. On the substance, the questions on variance reduction should be addressed more deeply, ideally both theoretically and from numerical simulations. For all these reasons, I recommend to reject this submission.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 2LN6
content.comment:
[Define problem / Tree size estimation vs. speeding up the computation time]: Thanks for raising this point! We noticed some places in the text where it wasn’t made clear that MCFS is an *offline* operation for training a policy and incurs no cost online when solving an instance. Our goal is to learn a branching policy for a given distribution of problem instances that minimizes average tree size. MCFS is a computationally-expensive offline procedure for finding small trees.  AlphaGo does MCTS both offline and online. As the reviewer points out, we cannot afford the computation time to do MCFS online. Exactly like AlphaGo, we train a deep-learning model based on the policy data from offline MCFS. 

[Construction/training of the neural networks missing]: We don’t describe in the main body but we do have a detailed description in the appendix (we mention this at the beginning Section 5). See Appendix B for a detailed description of our architecture / hyper params and training procedure. We will move into the main text for the final submission.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) based approach to guiding DPLL SAT solvers to find small proof trees for UNSAT instances. Since the size of a proof tree is determined by the order of branching variables used in the DPLL algorithm, the essential problem is to find the optimal policy, i.e., a sequence of branching variables that result in the smallest proof tree. The key technical contribution is to properly estimate the value of a state (i.e., the size of the decision/proof tree to show the current instance is UNSAT), for which this paper uses a mixed method -- a neural network is used in the first L branching decisions, and then a sub-solver (e.g., existing SAT solvers) is used to get the precise number of decisions, $V_{sub}$. Then, based on the Knuth sampling method, the total number of decisions can be estimated as $2^L*V_{sub} + 2^L -1$.  This paper also chooses a proper representation to capture important structural invariants like permutations of clauses and literals. The experimental evaluation on synthetic UNSAT instances shows that the MCTS-guided approach helps to find relatively smaller proof trees and sometimes achieves slightly better runtime performance.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- this paper presents an exciting motivation and illustrates the proposed approach in a clear and thorough manner
- this paper tries to address an important and challenging problem (i.e., finding small proofs of UNSAT) from an interesting angle (i.e., guiding DPLL with MCTS)
- the experimental evaluation uses a non-trivial baseline (i.e., kcnfs07) and relatively strong benchmarks

Weaknesses: 
- the general idea of using MCTS to guide search is not very new
- the proposed approach only helps to solve UNSAT instances, however, the satisfiability of which may not be known in advance
- It's not clear whether the proof tree is indeed the smallest one
- the improvement is not very significant, especially for larger instances
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Monte Carlo Tree Search is a well-known technique, and the particular application of MCTS for guiding DPLL algorithm for UNSAT instances is novel.  The authors also make interesting adaptions of MCTS for finding small UNSAT proof trees. This work is easy to reproduce with the supplemental materials (i.e., source code and testing data).
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper makes interesting technical contributions for UNSAT solving, which has quite fewer explorations in machine learning community (compared to SAT solving), but the experimental evaluation only shows modest improvement over the baseline.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper5575 by Reviewer ZSJE

content.title: Response to Reviewer ZSJE
content.comment:
Thank you for your review. We’re glad you liked the paper. We provide a few comments about the weaknesses you mention.

[MCTS to guide search is not very new]: We agree that there are many use cases of MCTS for search. However, we are not aware of any examples of using MCTS to (1) guide searching for a tree rather than a path or (2) offline train a branching policy for CSP problems in the AlphaGo style.

[Only works on UNSAT problems, which may not be known in advance]: There are many examples of specialized algorithms for the SAT or UNSAT case. For example, local search is a very well-studied class of algorithms and cannot prove UNSAT. In practice, you can always use a portfolio strategy where you run a specialized SAT and UNSAT algorithm in parallel and terminate if either finds a solution of a proof tree. 

[Not clear whether the proof tree is indeed the smallest one]: That’s correct. We provide no guarantees that we find the smallest tree. We would like to find small enough trees such that we can learn an approximation to these policies that improves upon existing branching heuristics. In practice we are able to find smaller trees than state-of-the-art heuristics.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a new algorithm, Monte-Carlo Forest Search (MCFS). Unlike MCTS, which is designed to find near-optimal *paths* in a search space (typically a MDP), MCFS is designed to find small trees. This is useful in problems like UNSAT where a single path is not sufficient, rather, the smallest tree must be constructed (as a proof of UNSAT) from a very large set of possible trees. The key idea is to learn a variable selection policy for use in the DPLL algorithm. Offline learning techniques popularized in AlphaGo are used. The main contributions are algorithmic and ,to a smaller extent, experimental. Experiments are conducted on standard UNSAT problem distributions. The results show some improvement in tree search size but struggle to outperform a strong baseline in terms of total runtime.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
  * The paper tackles an important problem. Speeding up complete search algorithms can benefit many applications.
  * The paper is technically correct and leverages well-studied, proven techniques from the MCTS literature.
  * The setup and approach has some novelty. 
  * The experiments are nicely detailed and comparisons against a strong baseline are included.

Weaknesses
  - The algorithmic contributions of the paper need to be made clearer. A large body of work exists on the offline learning of control knowledge in search / planning, which includes MCTS as a sub-area. It's currently unclear which of the techniques described here are novel. Something novel may be happening with the use of Knuth sampling and the tree-size based cost function in anytime search but I'm not sure.
  - I had difficulty understanding the details of the optimization problem in Section 4.2 (e.g., cost function and Q value update). To me, this is the key algorithmic contribution of the paper and while I think I have an intuitive understanding of the idea, I'd have preferred to understand it in more detail. An illustrative example, perhaps expanding Figure 1 with numerical details illustrating Section 4.2, might make this important part of the paper easier to understand.
  - The experiments are conducted carefully, which is nice. However, the reduction in tree size is offset in 7 of 8 cases by slower total runtime compared to kcnfs07. Considering that kcnfs07 is based on a heuristic and does not require additional GPU hardware or costly offline learning steps, it becomes hard to see the improvement of MCFS in UNSAT. Although I consider negative results valuable, I think the paper doesn't contain enough analytical discussion or insights.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity
  * The paper is reasonably well written. However, it could benefit from a more formal description of the problem formulation and an illustrative example of the key ideas (e.g., Section 4.2).

Quality
  * The main ideas seem technnically sound. The experimentn are carefully conducted and include strong baselines.

Novelty
  * I think the paper may have some algorithmic novelty but it needs to be made clearer as mentioned above.

Reproducibility
  * Search speedup experiments with offline learnning components are generally not easy to reproduce. The authors have provided code and a good amount of implementationn details. I have no reason to doubt the reproducibility of the experiments.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The proposed approach for learning search control knowledge to speedup DPLL search in UNSAT is sound in principle but the cost of knowledge is found to be too high compared to a strong baseline. Insufficient algorithmic novelty, experimental gains or insights make it difficult to recommend acceptance.

-----

UPDATE: I thank the authors for their response. While there is a bit more clarity about the contributions, the overall novelty still seems limited to me. Other concerns remain unaddressed (e.g., significance of empirical results). Since the primary contribution of the paper is algorithmic and empirical, the overall contribution remains insufficient, in my opinion.

content.title: Response to Reviewer WMiN
content.comment:
[Clarify which points are novel]: Thank you for this feedback. On reflection, we noticed many places in the paper where we could improve clarity. Notably, we have substantially restructured the text in the methods section (Section 4) to better outline our contributions and improve understanding. We now summarize our contributions:

Monte Carlo Forest Search (MCFS) is the first algorithm for finding small search trees that leverages the benefits of MCTS. We are also the first to use an AlphaGo-like approach (offline MCTS procedure) for training a tree-search branching policy.  MCTS is suitable when a policy can be evaluated with a path. It wasn’t clear how to do that when a policy creates a tree. The three main pieces of MCFS are:
1. Knuth samples. We recognized that a Knuth sample allows us to evaluate the tree size  (our cost function) of a policy with path-based rollouts from root to leaf, which allows us to directly leverage MCTS approaches.
2. We bound the number of policy calls by only training on top-level decisions. At test time, we need to build out the entire proof tree to prove unsatisfiability. It is too expensive to call our deep neural network policy for every node of a tree of potentially exponential size. For lower-level decisions, we leverage an existing SAT solver at both training time and test time.
2. We needed to scale confidence intervals $U(s,a)$ according to depth because of the tree-size cost function. Our $Q$ values for a node represent the tree size below that node. Tree size below a given node decreases exponentially with the depth of the node. Since (1) $Q$ values scale exponentially with decreasing node depth in our setting and (2) confidence intervals $U(s,a)$ are only a function of counts and don't scale with rewards/cost, we needed to scale $U$ values with depth. In AlphaZero, $Q$ values preserve scale with depth, where -1 represents a loss and 1 represents a win, therefore $Q$ will always be on the same scale as $U$ at every node. We multiply $U(s,a)$ by $Q_{d}$, the average $Q$ value for nodes at depth $d$. This prevents us from trading off tight confidence intervals at shallow nodes with loose confidence intervals at deeper nodes.

Can you see the novelty of our approach given this clarification?

[Better explanation in Section 4.2 (Cost function and $Q$ value update)]: See point (3) above.
